title: Why Every Snap Investor Is Looking At This One Number
detail:
Why Every Snap Investor Is Looking At This One Number

Image from Pixabay

Investors buying Snap (SNAP) stock may be betting on a surprising part of the business: the subscriptions it sells directly to users. Most people still consider Snap an advertising company, but a growing portion of its revenue now comes straight from its audience. The stock lost 28% over the past twelve months, contrasting with a 17.0% return for the S&P 500. So, how many of Snapchat's users actually pay for it?

Less Than 3% Of Snap's Monthly Users Pay

Snapchat had 971 million monthly active users in the second quarter of fiscal 2026. Less than 3% of them were paying subscribers. Executives provided both figures on the company's August earnings call.

Subscriptions lead a business segment that already generates real money. Snap's revenue outside advertising grew 85% to $316 million in the quarter. Executives said Snapchat+, Memory Storage, and the Lens+ subscription led that growth.

Advertising is still the dominant business, but its expansion is much slower. Ad revenue rose 9% to $1.28 billion in the same quarter. So revenue outside advertising accounted for about a fifth of Snap's $1.6 billion total, making it the faster-growing side of the company.

Is Snap Getting Closer To A Profit?

The figures of the past three years suggest it is, although Snap still loses money. Its net loss was 4.9% of revenue over the last twelve months, compared with a 13.3% profit margin for the S&P 500. That loss remains a central concern for investors.

The loss has shrunk every year. It was 30% of revenue three years ago and 24% two years ago, before narrowing to 9.7% a year ago. Snap is also already bringing in cash. Executives noted the company has generated positive free cash flow for eight consecutive quarters.

Management expects the financial improvement to continue. On the August call, executives said the company expects sustained positive net income beginning in 2027. They also expect the money users pay directly to keep growing materially faster than the business as a whole.

There is room for expansion. Management said app subscription penetration seems to be typically around 7% to 12% over the long term, well above Snapchat's share today. This range was offered as a comparison, not a forecast for Snapchat itself.

Snap cannot rely on subscriptions alone yet, and its expenses are rising. The company raised its forecast for full-year infrastructure costs to $1.65 billion to $1.70 billion, up from $1.60 billion to $1.65 billion previously.

What Could Stop More Snapchat Users From Paying?

title: Is It Too Late To Buy Shopify Stock?
detail:
Is It Too Late To Buy Shopify Stock?
Trefis Team

SHOP
^GSPC
META
LSPD
ADBE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Shopify (SHOP) stock has risen 34.3% over the past three months, while the S&P 500 gained 2.8%. On September 22, the shares rose about 8% in early trading after Meta connected its Muse AI agent to Shopify's Shop Pay checkout. Investors buying the stock today pay for all of it. So how much does a buyer pay for Shopify's business after that rise?

Shopify Costs Far More Than The Market

The stock trades at 16.7 times its sales over the past twelve months, compared with a multiple of 3.1 for the S&P 500. Over the past ten years, this multiple has ranged from 6.5 to 54.2. Today's valuation remains well below the top of that historical range.

Shopify also costs far more than the market based on profit and cash. The stock trades at 114.8 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. It also trades at 93.1 times operating cash flow, compared with 14.7 for the broader index.

Investors paying that price are acquiring a business that converts a larger portion of each sale into operating profit. Over the past twelve months, Shopify recorded an operating margin of 17.8%, up from 15.3% a year earlier. This marks the highest operating margin for the company in ten years. Payments are also contributing a growing share of the business. During the second quarter of 2026, Shopify's payments service handled 68% of the value of goods sold through its merchants' stores, up 3 points from a year earlier.

How Fast Does Shopify Have To Keep Growing?

Shopify has increased its revenue by more than 30% from a year earlier in each of its last four quarters. For the second quarter of 2026, revenue growth came in at 33.7%.

The company generates more revenue as its merchants increase their own sales. In the second quarter, the value of goods sold through merchant stores rose 32%. That marked the fifth straight quarter with growth above 30%.

Current share prices appear to assume that Shopify will continue growing its sales by more than 30% a year. Management has only guided to that pace for one quarter, the third quarter, which ended on September 30 and has not been reported yet. During their August 5, 2026 earnings call, executives said they expected third-quarter revenue growth in the low 30s.

Executives were less definitive regarding cash generation. When asked on the call whether a free cash flow margin of roughly 20% represented a new normal, management declined to confirm it. They pointed instead to their third-quarter guide, which forecasts a margin in the high teens to low 20s.

Shopify Stock Has Gone Both Ways On Its Results

title: Is Walmart Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?
detail:
Is Walmart Stock Increasing Your Market Risk?
Trefis Team
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 2:09 PM PDT 4 min read
WMT
^GSPC
AMZN
COST
TGT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Investors often hold Walmart (WMT) stock alongside funds that already track the S&P 500. Walmart is a retailer of groceries and everyday essentials worth about $886 billion. A stock that moves in lockstep with the broader index simply compounds existing bets, while one that charts its own course helps spread risk. So what does Walmart stock do on the market's good days and bad days?

Walmart Stock Has Gone Its Own Way

Over the past year, Walmart shares have not compounded broader market risk. Consider a $10,000 position in Walmart stock. On an average day when the S&P 500 rose over the past year, the index gained 0.65% while the retail shares ended the day about $1 lower. Conversely, on an average day when the index fell, the index dropped 0.6% and the shares finished about $10 higher. Distilled to a single metric, Walmart stock moved about 0.04% in the opposite direction for each 1% the index moved. That translates to almost no link at all.

This lack of correlation does not mean the investment is calm. Over the past year, its volatility, defined as the size of its typical swings, was 27%, against 13.0% for the S&P 500. Walmart swung about twice as widely as the benchmark index, yet it did not move in step with it. Holding the stock introduces risk, but it remains a separate one from the risk embedded in index funds.

Can Walmart's Steady Sales Prolong This Pattern?

The underlying business suggests this pattern will persist, with the stock trading on company-specific developments rather than broader market sentiment. Over the past year, Walmart's correlation with the index, a measure of how often the two move together, was -0.02. That means the two barely move together.

Operations remain steady. Revenue grew between 5.6% and 7.3% from a year earlier in each of the past four quarters. During the company's August 20, 2026 earnings call, management raised its forecast for sales growth in the current fiscal year, measured in constant currency. Executives now expect a range of 4% to 5%, up from prior estimates of 3.5% to 4.5%.

Investors pay a high price for that stability. Walmart stock is priced at 40.1 times earnings, against the 21.9 multiple for the S&P 500. On that same call, management acknowledged that lapping 19% growth in earnings per share will be a challenge next year. Given its current valuation, a disappointing quarter could trigger sharp price movements regardless of how the broader market performs. Consequently, wide swings of its own are likely to continue.

title: Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: UPS vs. Energy Transfer
detail:
Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: UPS vs. Energy Transfer
Roxanna Maglangit
Mon, October 12, 2026 at 1:08 PM PDT 5 min read
UPS
AMZN
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Better High-Yield Dividend Stock: UPS vs. Energy Transfer ©Alesia Kozik from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

UPS yields 7.0% and Energy Transfer yields 6.8%, so $10,000 pays $700 or $680 a year today.

UPS paid out 99% of its free cash flow as dividends over the 12 months to June 2026, and analysts expect 96% for fiscal 2026.

Energy Transfer's distributable cash flow covered its distribution 1.78x in fiscal 2025, with 2.11x expected for fiscal 2026, though it carries far more debt than UPS.

UPS's fiscal 2025 dividend raise was 0.6% and Energy Transfer's was 4.7%, and Energy Transfer targets 3% to 5% a year.

On July 28, United Parcel Service (UPS:NYSE) said it had finished pushing lower-yielding Amazon volume out of its network, and raised its 2026 outlook. A week later, Energy Transfer (ET) posted record volumes and raised its own.

Both stocks also yield close to 7%. But a big yield is only as good as the cash behind it.

So which is the better high-yield dividend stock?

UPS has a turning business and a stretched payout

CEO Carol Tomé told investors on the July 28 call that "this reconfiguration was never the destination. It was the foundation." Second-quarter 2026 revenue rose 7.6% to $22.8 billion, from $21.2 billion a year earlier, and management raised its full-year revenue outlook to about $91.2 billion.

The dividend is a tighter fit. UPS paid out a stretched 99% of its free cash flow over the 12 months to June 30, 2026. Consensus puts fiscal 2026 at 96%, as free cash flow climbs 18%, from $4.77 billion in fiscal 2025 to $5.64 billion. That estimate looks solid: 10 analysts make it, and management targets about $5.5 billion. But management also plans around $5.4 billion of dividends this year, which leaves almost nothing over.

Dividends paid outran free cash flow in fiscal 2023 and again in fiscal 2025, when $5.40 billion went out against $4.77 billion…

United Parcel Service (UPS): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

…and the raises have slowed. Fiscal 2025's raise was 0.6%, well off the 10.2% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025, and there's been none since: the dividend has been $1.64 a quarter since February 2025. With so little left over, the dividend leans on the turnaround delivering.

Energy Transfer's cushion comes with more debt

Where UPS is stretching to cover its dividend, Energy Transfer has cash to spare. Second-quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA rose 31% to $5.07 billion, from $3.87 billion a year earlier, on record NGL volumes. It's an MLP, so it pays distributions on units, with a K-1 at tax time.

Distributable cash flow covered the distribution a comfortable 1.78x in fiscal 2025, at $2.38 a unit against $1.34. Consensus sees 2.11x for fiscal 2026, as distributable cash flow per unit rises 21% to $2.89. The raised guidance backs that up, and last year's consensus came within 2% of the actual.
